name: South Slavey
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file
sweep_summary: South Slavey is not in the catalog. The single sweep item, Rice 1987 'Metrical structure in a tone language: the foot in Slave (Athapaskan)', resolves to CLS 23 vol. 2 pp. 239-252 (citation confirmed from four bibliographies) and to ANLA typescript CA976Rc1987 (ca. 27 pp., languages 'Comparative Athabaskan, Hare, Slave', no file); Glottolog's ANLA URL is dead, and no open copy exists (HathiTrust, archive.org, Crossref, Google Books no-preview) — only its first sentence was readable, and the foot argument is probably Hare-based, so relevance to South Slavey stress is unclear (priority medium). The best first-hand statement found is Rice 2010 (Survey of Word Accentual Patterns, pp. 171-172), assembled from Google Books snippets: 'In the South Slavey dialect, quantity distinctions have generally been neutralized, and accent is on the stem vowel... The stem vowel is stressed, whether a suffix is present or not', citing Rice 1989 as data source and contrasting Hare. Rice 1989 A Grammar of Slave p. 46 (snippets copied from the slav1253 folder) says stress is not distinctive in Slave and gives the pre-stem/stem rule for Hare only. A South Slavey record would be 'morphological, stem-vowel stress (non-distinctive, intensity-cued)', consistent with the recode already recommended for the sister Slave record slav1253. Everything fetched sources is under with. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and Google Books API v1 were rate-limited, so the Google Books feed endpoint was used instead.

new_statements.quote: In Slave, too, the stem plays an important role in determining accent placement. In the South Slavey dialect, quantity distinctions have generally been neutralized, and accent is on the stem vowel. The stem vowel is underlined; an acute accent marks high tone, and the hyphen indicates a stem boundary. (23) South Slavey (dialect of Slave; data from Rice 1989 unless otherwise indicated) a. ch-'ke 'boy' b. 'lu-e 'fish' c. ne-'do 'you sg. drink' d. de-'tsil-e ... The stem vowel is stressed, whether a suffix is present or not (23b, d, e), and whether that suffix ends in a consonant (23e) or a vowel (23b, d). In the Hare dialect of Slave the position of accent differs in nouns and verbs. Nouns are accented on the stem (24a), as in South Slavey; verbs have prestem accent, as in (24b)

new_statements.rule_in_words: South Slavey word accent (stress) is morphologically fixed: it falls on the stem (root) vowel of nouns and verbs alike, regardless of whether a suffix follows; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed. Rice 2018 (p. 232, snippet) restates this as prominence on the first syllable of the root, with no weight sensitivity because historical vowel-length contrasts have been neutralized. The reference grammar (Rice 1989:46) adds that stress is not distinctive in Slave and that a prefix vowel bearing a floating plus lexical high tone gets extra intensity.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed in Rice 2010. Rice 1983 (Fort Nelson Slave report, pp. 17-18, full scan on file) describes 'alternating stress' from the stem-initial syllable rightward (both syllables of disyllabic words stressed, possessive prefixes skipped, suffix stressed only when non-phrase-final); Rice 2018 table p. 250 codes Slavey as 'syllabic trochee' on the root.
new_statements.exceptions: Hare (North Slavey) verbs have prestem accent instead (Rice 2010:172; Rice 1989:46; Hargus & Rice 2005:35). Rice 1989:46: stress is not a distinctive feature in Slave; a prefix vowel with lexical high tone that also receives a shifted high tone 'has extra stress, or is more intense'; in Fort Nelson Slave possessive prefixes are ignored 'for most speakers' and suffixes are unstressed phrase-finally (Rice 1983:17-18).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stems with prefixes and suffixes; nouns and verbs); Rice 1983 additionally notes phrase-position effects on suffix stress. Rice is the field linguist for all Slave dialects and the 2010 chapter uses her own grammar data (Rice 1989), so the statement is first-hand although it appears in a typological survey chapter. Text recovered from overlapping Google Books snippet windows saved to disk, not from a page scan; the two deciding sentences are complete in the windows.
new_statements.identity_note: Rice 2010's 'South Slavey (dialect of Slave)' is the NWT Slavey of Fort Simpson/Dehcho, i.e. sout2959; her grammar (Rice 1989) and the 1993 sketch cover the whole Slave dialect complex (South Slavey, Bearlake, Hare, Mountain; the audit's family-level directory is slav1253, and Hare/Bearlake/Mountain = North Slavey nort2942). The full-scan first-hand stress description on file (Rice 1983, Part 4) is for Fort Nelson Slave, the British Columbia dialect of South Slavey (Fort Nelson, Kahntah, Fontas), which Rice says differs from NWT Slavey in several features; the StressTyp2 'Slave' entry and Gordon 2016 report the Hare (North Slavey) verb pattern as if it were general Slave.

new_statements.reading: South Slavey word stress/accent is morphologically fixed on the stem vowel: the (typically final or near-final) stem syllable is stressed whether or not a suffix follows, and syllable weight plays no role because quantity contrasts have been neutralised. Written by Keren Rice, the primary describer of Slave, citing her own 1989 grammar as the data source; reachable only as overlapping Google Books snippets (pp. 171-172), so the full example set (23a-e) should be read from the chapter itself. Rice 1989 p. 46 adds that stress is not distinctive in Slave and that intensity is its main correlate, and describes a different pre-stem-verb / stem-noun pattern for the Hare dialect (North Slavey), which Rice 2010 also contrasts with South Slavey.

sources.quote: Stress is not a distinctive feature [in] Slave. In the Hare dialect, there are stress-like properties which are predictable. What might be called stress generally falls on the vowel immediately preceding the stem of a verb and on the stem vowel of a noun. A stressed vowel is generally acoustically more intense than an unstressed vowel, and intensity is in fact the primary phonetic correlate of stress. See chapter 8. In prefixes in all dialects, a high tone may fall on a vowel with lexical high tone. That vowel then has extra stress, or is more intense.
